paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Growing up on the north side of Charlotte, North Carolina, Anthony Foxx remembers an imposing brick wall at the end of the block. On the side was a high-speed entrance ramp that connected two highways. For Foxx, the wall, the highways, and the hum of traffic blended into the background. Over time, however, he came to understand they weren’t part of the neighborhood at all. ‘Those freeways were there to carry people through my neighborhood, but never to my neighborhood,’ said Foxx, a senior employee of the US Department of Transportation (DOT). It hadn’t always been that way. When his grandparents purchased the house on Crestdale Drive in 1961, it connected with surrounding streets. But soon after, the federal government placed the path of new highways through the established neighborhood. Houses were demolished. Local businesses were relocated and property values diminished.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: As DOT secretary, Foxx implemented a program to identify and fix urban areas where highways have isolated communities. Foxx believes that these communities reflect the values of the past – that in the US, there were some people who were accepted within society, and others who were not. ‘I think we’ve got to have a different idea in the 21st century,’ Foxx explained.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Federal officials have visited several cities to gather input from urban planners, architects and community members, and help them envision ways to reconnect neighborhoods dominated by highways. Those visions include building public spaces on top of roads, lowering elevated structures to ground level, or removing the roads altogether. In central Philadelphia a side road connected to a major highway, the Interstate 676 spur, has blocked three neighborhoods from receiving economic investments and prevented residents from accessing local parks. When DOT officials visited the city, Philadelphia mayor Jim Kenney remarked that, ‘they took the time to walk the crosswalks and to hear the noise of I-676 and to feel the hard line that it draws through the community.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Concern for communities isn’t the only reason highways are being modified or removed. Sometimes they have simply become worn out. When President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, it was the first time the federal government contributed an initial $25 billion toward the construction of more than 41,000 new miles of roadways. Federal officials paid for 90 percent of project costs, asking state and local governments to cover the rest. The US, however, has largely stopped funding and fixing its infrastructure. When highways reach the end of their useful life these days it is often cheaper to remove them.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Cost was the main factor when the city of San Francisco had to decide whether to replace the Embarcadero Freeway. When an earthquake damaged the structure, San Francisco city officials chose to pay $49 million to remove it rather than S69.5 million to replace it. The elevated highway was replaced with a six-lane boulevard surrounded by a 25-foot-wide pedestrian promenade. Available housing in the area increased by 51 percent in the five years after crews completed the project, and property values in the adjacent neighborhoods increased 300 percent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: In Milwaukee, Wisconsin, construction on the elevated Park East Freeway, initially intended as a three-mile link between Lake Michigan and Milwaukee’s southern suburbs, began in 1971. One year later, it stopped. Both community opposition and high construction costs left the project at a standstill, with only one phase finished. When voters elected John Norquist mayor in 1977, it was in no small part based on his opposition to completing the highway. ‘[It] would have killed Milwaukee,’ said Norquist, who added that the city’s population would be ‘much lower’ now if the highway had been completed. At a cost of $25 million. Park East was removed in 2003. Keeping the highway would have cost an additional $50 to $80 million. By 2006, the average assessed land values in the Park East area had grown by 180 percent. Streets reconnected on the local traffic grid. Developers created three new neighborhoods on the land, which brought in roughly $250 million in investments.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Milwaukee inspired other projects. Boston’s Big Dig project put the city’s main traffic route into a tunnel and opened more than 300 acres of space above when it was completed in 2007. In the city of Dallas, Klyde Warren Park – a 5.2-acre public space on top of Woodall Rodgers Freeway – was built between 2009 and 2012.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: ‘The idea of tearing these things down is still pretty new, and for a lot of people, still pretty weird,’ said Norquist. ‘Their first reaction is, “You want to do what?”.’ The belief is that, without highways, traffic will come to a standstill. Businesses will suffer. Yet after the demolition of these highways, major traffic spikes never materialized. Why? This is because a highway ‘concentrates the traffic’ in urban areas, said Norquist. He explained that while highways offer value in carrying vehicles long distances at high rates of speed, they’re inefficient in a city environment, where traffic forms around on-ramps and exits. In a 2011 study conducted at the University of Connecticut. Jason Billings suggested that street grids of most cities had been underutilized because of urban highways, and, after the demolition of the highways, proved able to absorb and disperse large amounts of traffic.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: The ongoing discussions about highway removals and relocations aren’t simply about traffic and transportation. They’re about the people whose lives were altered by the mid-century construction of highways. For the first time in the 60 years since the interstate highways arrived, city inhabitants are at last seeing the restoration of their neighborhoods.
